transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I keep getting these sudden, vivid memories of the train crash that pop into my head and completely derail whatever I’m doing. It happened a little over two years ago, but it still feels like it's happening right now when those memories hit.
Do you experience these vivid memories as a form of flashback, where you feel like you're reliving the train crash, or are they more like recurring, distressing thoughts about the event?

They definitely feel like actual flashbacks where my brain just hijacks me and I'm suddenly right back in that dark, tilted train car. It's so vivid that I can hear the screaming and smell the smoke, completely losing track of where I am—like during a Zoom meeting where I have to mute myself just to try and pull it together.
Have you been avoiding people, places, or activities that remind you of the train crash, or is it mainly these flashbacks that are causing you distress?

It’s definitely both, and they are both causing me massive distress. I’ve completely restructured my life to avoid anything train-related, like driving an extra hour in traffic to avoid the Metro-North and changing the TV channel if a subway scene comes on. At the same time, the flashbacks are incredibly disruptive, hijacking my brain while I’m coding or in Zoom meetings and making me completely lose track of what I'm doing.
Do you find yourself constantly on edge, easily startled by sudden noises, or do you have difficulty falling or staying asleep due to feeling constantly 'on guard'?

Yes, I'm constantly on edge and find myself flinching at sudden sounds like loudspeaker announcements or crossing bells. It makes sleeping almost impossible—I lie awake wired until two or three in the morning bracing for an impact, and when I finally fall asleep, I just jerk awake from train nightmares.
Can you tell me more about how these feelings of being 'on edge' affect your daily life, such as your ability to concentrate or your relationships with others?

I'm so exhausted from being constantly on guard and barely sleeping that I can't concentrate or think straight at work. It's also ruining my relationships because my fuse is incredibly short; I'll snap at my boyfriend if he's just five minutes late or fire off really sharp messages to my coworkers, and then I feel deeply ashamed afterward.
Have you also been experiencing feelings of guilt, shame, or self-blame related to the train crash, or is it more the anxiety and fear that are driving your avoidance and distress?

I definitely carry a lot of self-blame, constantly replaying that night and thinking if I hadn't stayed late or had pulled the emergency brake, I could have stopped it. I feel so stupid for ever thinking I was in control, but the sheer anxiety and fear of trains are also huge drivers of my daily distress.
When you experience these flashbacks, do you feel like you're observing yourself from outside your body or like you're detached from the world around you?

No, I don't feel detached or like I'm watching myself from the outside at all. It actually feels the exact opposite—it's incredibly real, and I get completely pulled back into the terrifying sensory details and physical sensations of the crash itself.
Have you ever felt like you're in a daze or spaced out, where things around you seem unreal or distant, especially when you're not having a flashback?

No, I don't really feel spaced out or like things are unreal when I'm not having a flashback. Outside of those moments, I'm usually just very tense and hyper-aware of everything around me rather than feeling distant.
Have you experienced any significant avoidance of thoughts, feelings, or conversations related to the train crash, in addition to avoiding places or activities that remind you of it?

I try as hard as I can to avoid thinking or talking about it, but those painful thoughts and feelings usually end up hijacking my mind anyway. Because of that, I rely heavily on avoiding physical reminders, like driving an extra hour to avoid the train, steering clear of stations, and even changing the TV channel if I hear train sounds. It's like I can control the physical reminders to some extent, but the internal thoughts are almost impossible to block out.
